summary: The note traces street art's shift from graffiti seen as vandalism to a gallery-recognized art form, citing pioneers like Basquiat and Haring and newer artists working with murals, AR, VR and eco-friendly materials. It covers shifting public perception, gallery exhibitions and rising market value (with the risk of assimilation), community education programs, and sustainability. It closes by speculating that street art will keep reinventing itself across physical and digital spaces.
one_line: Street art has evolved from rebellious graffiti into a gallery-validated, tech-integrated and eco-conscious movement with educational and commercial dimensions.
key_facts: In the 1970s and 1980s, Jean-Michel Basquiat and Keith Haring took their messages from New York subways to esteemed galleries.
On October 12, 2023, street artist Elara Montesinos unveiled sweeping murals across the historic district of L.A., resonating with Basquiat's raw, emotive power.
Alexandra Kovacs and Finnegan Yue were cited in the 'Art of the Streets' exhibition on November 18, 2023.
Alexandra Kovacs creates surreal landscapes across the metallic surfaces of derelict buildings, while Finnegan Yue makes interactive 3D murals incorporating augmented reality.
Critic James Holloway called street art "the most important art movement of the 21st century" during a seminar on December 5, 2023.
Educational institutions have integrated street art into their curriculum, and city councils collaborate with artists to beautify urban areas.
At the 'Virtual Visions' showcase on January 22, 2024, Jenzo Harmon presented a virtual reality mural that adapted to the emotions of its interactors.

The 'Urban Narratives' exhibition on February 15, 2024, brought street art into conversation with fine art; curator Mika Saito said gallery display contrasts the rawness of outdoor work against a sterile environment.

Street artists like Rafael Gomez moving to galleries see their works fetch prices rivaling established contemporary artists, but the commercial success risks assimilating a counterculture into the establishment.
'Paint the Future', initiated on March 3, 2024, partners artists with local youth to create murals on social issues.
Artist-educator Maya Torres leads a workshop series, emphasizing street art's inherent accessibility.
Zachary Liu developed bio-degradable sprays and solar-powered LED installations; his series 'Nature on Concrete' uses non-toxic materials and decays naturally over time.
Digital graffiti uses light projections instead of permanent paint to create ephemeral works.
